planting.note: Direct sow 1-2 inches deep once soil has warmed well past last frost; this sprawling heirloom rewards a long, hot season, so Gulf Coast gardeners can sow successively from late spring into midsummer.

directions: Direct sow into warm, well-drained soil and allow the sprawling vines room to run, since this variety spreads farther than bush-type cowpeas. Clay is a historic Southern cowpea type, named for the earthy, clay-brown color of its dry seed, stewarded by African American seed-keeping families since at least 1867 and valued for producing a hearty, protein-rich dry pea as well as tender snap-stage pods. It tolerates poor, droughty soils and fixes nitrogen for whatever crop follows. Harvest young for fresh shelling or let pods dry fully on the vine for long-term storage.

planting.note: Direct sow 1-2 inches deep after soil has warmed to at least 65°F; this pre-1860 Southern heirloom thrives through the hottest weeks of a Gulf Coast summer.

directions: Direct sow into average garden soil and keep watered through flowering and pod set for the best yields, though established plants tolerate real dry spells. Blue Goose is a rare, richly flavored Southern heirloom cowpea dating from before 1860, named for its distinctive purple-gray seed packed roughly fifteen to a pod. Young pods can be snapped and cooked like green beans, and the tender leaves are edible as a cooked potherb similar to spinach. Let pods dry on the vine for a hearty, nitrogen-fixing dry pea crop.

planting.note: Direct sow 1 inch deep near a trellis or fence after soil has warmed; this running, semi-climbing heirloom needs support to produce its best in a Gulf Coast garden.

directions: Direct sow near a trellis, fence, or other support, since this cowpea runs and climbs rather than staying in a tidy bush. Holstein takes its name from the striking black-and-white mottled pattern on its seed, reminiscent of the dairy cow's coat, and was recorded under the older name Polecat in an 1860s survey of Southern cowpea varieties. Vigorous vines bear pods of ten to twelve peas that are excellent picked green for fresh shelling or left to dry for storage. Like other cowpeas it fixes nitrogen and tolerates heat and humidity better than most legumes.

planting.note: Direct sow after soil is reliably warm; give this tall-growing West African okra plenty of vertical space and a long Gulf Coast season to size up.

directions: Soak seed and direct sow into warm, fertile soil, allowing room for a very tall plant that can tower well over most garden okra by late summer. Moody Family is a distinct West African okra species, Abelmoschus caillei, rather than the common garden okra, stewarded for generations by an African American family carrying it forward from West African ancestors. Pink-tinged stems carry long, light green pods that blush pink at the tip and stay tender at a larger size than typical okra. Harvest regularly for frying and gumbo, and keep picking to sustain production through the hottest months.

planting.note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed and soil has warmed; this medium-height heirloom fits well in beds where taller okra would shade neighboring crops.

directions: Direct sow an inch deep into warm, well-drained soil in full sun. James Hopper is a preservation-collection heirloom valued for its moderate, manageable height compared to rangier Southern okra types, making it easier to harvest without a ladder in a home garden. Plants set standard green pods of 3-5 inches with reliable, steady production through the summer. Pick frequently once pods reach 3-4 inches for the most tender texture, since this variety can fiber up quickly if left too long between pickings.

planting.note: Direct sow after soil warms; Pentagreen tolerates cooler soil and air temperatures better than most okra, giving Gulf Coast gardeners a wider early-season sowing window.

directions: Direct sow into warm soil in full sun; Pentagreen stays notably compact compared to most Southern okra varieties while still producing heavily once plants begin branching early in the season. Pods are sharply five-angled and medium green, best picked at around 3 inches since they are slower to develop fiber than many varieties, giving a longer harvest window at any given size. This variety is unusually tolerant of cool conditions for an okra, making it productive even during cooler spring and fall stretches in zone 9a. Keep picking continuously through summer to keep plants flowering heavily.

planting.note: Direct sow after frost danger has passed; this early, compact Greek heirloom begins setting pods sooner than most Southern okra varieties.

directions: Direct sow an inch deep into warm soil in full sun. Elinitsa is a century-old heirloom from a small village in Greece, grown there for generations before being preserved and distributed through seed-saving networks. The spineless, slender green pods carry a mild, delicate flavor, and the plants are noticeably more compact and far less bristly or itchy to handle than many Southern okra varieties, making harvest more pleasant in the heat. It begins producing earlier than most okra, giving a head start on the summer harvest before the big Southern heirlooms hit their stride.
